the magnitude of changes needed at the synaptic to explain the observed changes in EPSP amplitude during LTP are consistent with a number of proposed mechanisms including increasing the numbers of receptors, unmasking of synapses, increasing vesicle release probability, and increasing the AMPA receptor conductance.

the average magnitude of LTP in CA1 pyramids in normal ACSF was 60%, and that this magnitude can be explained by a 60% increase in the probability of release, a 60% to 80% increase in AMPA single channel conductivity, or a 50% to 100% increase in AMPAR density per synapse.
the average increase in EPSC amplitude observed in CA1 pyramids with LTP is 60% and can be explained by a 64% average increase in the AMPAR single channel conductance.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the synaptic level mechanisms that are most likely to be sufficient to explain the experimental data include increasing AMPA receptor single-channel conductance and vesicle release probability, and a combination of increasing the numbers of activated synapses and AMPA receptor single- channel conductance.
LTP is a result of a combination of mechanisms, and that increasing AMPA receptor conductance is an important contributor to the synaptic change.

the magnitude of LPT can be explained by increases in the number or conductance of AMPA receptors and/or vesicle release probability, and that these changes are likely to occur in a cell-specific and stimulus-dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to use a combination of modeling and experiments to quantify the changes at the synaptic level needed to explain experimental results.
it is possible to use detailed models and whole cell recordings to estimate quantitively the changes in synaptic parameters that are required to explain experimental results.
it is possible to quantitatively estimate the synaptic level changes needed to explain LTP and to compare these changes to the changes predicted by different mechanisms.
